Michelangelo intended to flip his overbearing boss, the Pope, "the bird", and get away with it, when he painted two cherubim giving "the fig" gesture on a little wall of the church, directly in the line of site of where the Pope would be kneeling at mass. And if the artist didn't intend to mean these things in his work, then the audience eventually discovered these meanings anyways, derived from the different elements of his visual language. You could paint a series of paintings, collaging letters and numbers onto the substrate as a purely graphic or aesthetic consideration, and some of those paintings are going to spell out different words or (significant) numbers to different audience members, depending on their background. And so, we discovered that art was saying something even when the author didn't intend to, because there is such a thing as visual language, even if some of us were only really intuitive about this language in the past.

And so good art today is often self-conscious of this visual language and it constrains or directs the "concept" of the piece to explore or comment upon contemporary issues. Bad art often uses this system to advocate uninformed or amateur positions in a given field (e.g. artist as amateur chef, artist as amateur engineer, etc.).
